Testimony of Angela Westhoff, President & CEO Maine Health Care Association
Testimony before the Committee on Health and Human Services In Support of LD 1243, An Act Regarding the Licensing of Assisted Living Facilities Friday, April 11, 2025
Senator Ingwersen and Representative Meyer as well as Distinguished Members of the Health and Human Services Committee:
My name is Angela Westhoff, and I serve as the President & CEO of the Maine Health Care Association. We represent approximately 200 nursing homes, assisted living centers, and residential care facilities across the state. Our mission is to empower members to ensure the integrity, quality, and sustainability of long term care in Maine.
I am pleased to provide written testimony in support of LD 1243, An Act Regarding the Licensing of Assisted Living Facilities. This bill would allow the Department of Health and Human Services to issue more than one license, at the same license level, at the same location to an applicant for an assisted living or residential care facility license so long as construction on the facility had begun prior to October 1, 2023.
Long term care providers that began construction to add more beds should not be caught in an administrative black hole. In the last session, the legislature passed a department bill that prevents newly licensed long term care providers from having more than one license of the same type in the same location. For decades, providers have provided quality care while operating with multiple licenses. However, MHCA did not oppose that bill for several reasons, including that already established providers could maintain their multi-license status.
Unfortunately, during the bill's drafting and implementation process, some providers were already undertaking major steps of facility expansion -- including obtaining approval and making

significant financial investments -- with the understanding that they could add additional beds under a distinct license. LD 1243 would allow these providers to finish construction, potentially secure the license level they had planned on, and provide access to more beds to meet the increasing demand for long term care supports and services for older adults.
Access to long term care in Maine is severely challenged. There have been over 50 nursing home and residential care facility closures or conversions to lower levels of care since 2014. Nearly 70% of older adults are likely going to need long term care services at some point during their lives. And our older adult population is going to expand significantly in the next several years.
As this Committee is aware, there is another bill pending (LD 979) that reflects the Department's major substantive rule making effort that would significantly alter the licensure rules, regulatory framework, and staffing requirements for all Assisted Living, Residential Care Facilities, and Private Non-Medical Institutions in Maine. At the public hearing for that bill, MHCA testified in strong opposition. The one-size-fits-all approach to treating all residential care providers (RCF Level I-IV and PNMI Level I-IV) the same is problematic, not to mention entirely unrealistic to assume providers can hire an additional 600+ caregivers. Even if these additional staff could be found, there is zero funding available to help providers recruit and hire more direct caregivers. If that bill passes as drafted, providers that were in the middle of construction would be forced to comply with a new set of regulations regardless of the number of beds they would be adding to their newly constructed facility. The proposed new regulations wipe out virtually all distinctions between levels of residential care and PNMIs.
At a time when access to care is dwindling, we should be removing administrative barriers for providers that are trying to meet demand and have no substantiated licensure violations. They are trusted caregivers in their communities and are seeking to make a difference.
Thank you for your time.

Re: LD 1243 - An Act Regarding the Licensing of Assisted Living Facilities

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information as you consider LD 1277, An Act Regarding Controlled Substances Prescription Monitoring Activities. ,. The intent of this bill is to create an exemption to the 2023 law that prohibited a building/facility from obtaining multiple small facility licenses instead of a single large facility license for projects that were already in process prior to the law's enactment.

The Division of Licensing is neither for nor against this bill and its intent to address specific mitigating
factors for a licensee such as the fact the licensee had obtained local government approval, permits and project commencement prior to the 131st Legislature session in which the law was heard as a bill and
subsequently passed.

The Division would like to offer an amendment to the Committee in order to ensure that specific factors are included in the proposed statute change should the bill pass; the Division offers the following language below in red font for your consideration as an amendment:

Sec. 1. 22 MRSA �7851, sub-�3-A, �B, as enacted by PL 2023, c. 176, �7, is amended to read:
B. The department may issue more than one license at the same license level to an applicant for an assisted living facility license or a residential care facility license that, on October 1, 2023, held more than one license at the same license level for services offered in the same location. The department may also issue more than one license at the same license level to an applicant for an assisted living facility license or a residential care facility license if the applicant obtained municipal government approval and permits as well as project financing approvals prior to the 131st Legislature's review of the 2023 law and that the licensee had begun construction, prior to October 1, 2023, on a facility at the same license level for services offered in the same location as long as there were no Quality of Care and Services or Resident Rights violations of the license substantiated prior to October 1, 2023.

Sincerely,
Bill Montejo Director Division of Licensing and Certification Maine Department of Health and Human Services

Thank you, Senators, Representatives and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee
My name is Cindy Strout and I am from Harrington, Maine within the great Washington County. I am a nurse and had the pleasure of being a former owner of two AFCHs. I currently oversee paperwork for my families' AFCHs as well as continue to work part time at Harrington Family Health Center. And....Jeff is my oldest son.
My letter is regarding the change in the law beginning October 1, 2023, that the department may not issue more than one license at the same level to an applicant for an assisted living facility or a residential care facility for services offered in the same location.
In 1993 lawmakers and health officials initiated a policy change and introduced the Adult Family Care Home models for our aging population. They were aimed to shift the focus from nursing homes to "more home-like, less institutional" alternative homes and were a pivotal move, driven by a severe budget crunch. I have been involved with Adult Family Care Homes since 1998, owning two licensed homes. I had the honor of taking care of my mother at home until she passed away in 1997. It was that heart touching experience that led me to decide to explore, then open an Adult Family Care Home. My first home was in Harrington. The Grace Home was licensed a Level III AFCH in 1998 and then a Level IV in 2000. In 2004,1 renovated my old family home in Franklin and licensed it as my second Level IVAFCH. The homes were 20 miles apart. There were challenges running/operating the home from a distance. I lived at The Grace Home and drove to Mountain Vista 3 or 4 days a week. I have always said it would have been better to have both homes under one roof. I would have been able to have more "eyes on/hands on" instead of the way I did it. Unfortunately, I experienced a family tragedy and sold both homes in 2012.
My solution...allow for the revision of the law and instead of penalizing facilities that operate within the rules and regulations, monitor and sanction the facilities that do not.
Again, thank you for your time and consideration for letting me briefly touch on a subject that is near and dear to my heart. It is greatly appreciated!
Respectfully,

Subject: Testimony in favor of LD 1277 "An Act Regarding Controlled Substances Prescription Monitoring Activities"
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Joe Anderson. I am a resident of Portland, a pediatric hospitalist in Lewiston, and I serve on the board of the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics. The Maine Chapter of the AAP is a professional organization representing 300 pediatricians and pediatric subspecialists working together to further our mission to improve the lives of children and adolescents in Maine. We ask that you vote Ought to Pass on LD 1277.
As pediatricians, we are committed to the health, safety, and dignity of every child in Maine. This includes children and adolescents who are transgender, nonbinary, or gender diverse. Gender-affirming care, which may include the use of testosterone as part of a carefully considered medical plan, is evidence-based, developmentally appropriate, and supported by every major medical organization in the United States, including the American Academy of Pediatrics.
The PDMP is a valuable tool in the fight against prescription drug misuse and diversion. It was initially created to address the opioid crisis and is a vitally important tool in that capacity. However, its scope and use must be continually evaluated to ensure that it does not inadvertently cause harm. Testosterone, while classified as a Schedule III controlled substance, is tracked on the PDMP due to its scheduling classification. Most illicit steroids are smuggled into the U.S. from abroad, according to the DEA1. As such, its inclusion in the PDMP is of minimal benefit in addressing illicit steroid use, and can inadvertently create a dangerous opportunity for misuse of health information.
Across the country, we are seeing growing efforts by government actors to interfere in the confidential, medically necessary care of transgender individuals. Last fall, a pediatrician was sued by the state of Texas for providing gender affirming care to minors2. These patients were all prescribed testosterone, and one could assume that the reason these patients were singled out (as opposed to other patients who may have been prescribed different medications) was because the state had access to testosterone prescription data through their PDMP. These actions have a chilling effect, not only on providers, who fear criminalization for following medical standards, but on the youth and families we serve, who may delay or avoid care out of fear that their personal medical information could be weaponized against them.

Removing testosterone from the PDMP would not diminish appropriate regulatory oversight. It maintains its Schedule III classification at the federal level but would simply recognize the legitimate privacy interests of patients whose care is under increasing political scrutiny. It would also support providers who are acting in good faith and in accordance with best practices, ensuring they are not exposed to legal or professional risk for doing the right thing.
There are also immediate concerns highlighting the need for this legislation today. The current administration has focused aggressively on the transgender community, and specifically on Maine's policy on transgender athletes. The President has released executive orders threatening institutions who provide gender affirming care by way of retracting federal research or education grants,3 and excluding employees of organizations who provide gender affirming care from being qualified to receive Public Service Loan Forgiveness.4 We fear that Maine physicians and healthcare systems could be a target of federal action in this arena, and the current prescribing data present on our state's PDMP puts them at risk.
Maine has a proud tradition of protecting patient autonomy, provider judgment, and the rights of marginalized communities. This bill is a necessary and measured step to uphold those values. The Maine AAP urges you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 1277 and ensure that transgender youth and their families can access medically necessary care without fear. Thank you for your leadership on this critical issue.
Sincerely,
Joe Anderson, DO, FAAP Advocacy Chair, Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics
1 Department of Justice/Drug Enforcement Administration Drug Fact Sheet: Steroids. Obtained from https://www.dea.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/Steroids-2020_0.pdf
2 Texas sues doctor for prescribing testosterone to transgender minors. (2024, October 17). Reuters. https://www.reuters.com/world/us/texas-sues-doctor-prescribing-testosterone-transgender-minors-202410-17/
3 Protecting children from chemical and surgical mutilation. (2025, January 28). The White House. https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/protecting-children-from-chemical-and-surgicalmutilation/

April 11, 2025

Testimony In Support of

LD 1243 -An Act Regarding the Licensing of Assisted Living Facilities
Good morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee. I am Representative Tiffany Strout from Harrington, representing the towns of Milbridge, Harrington, Columbia, Columbia Falls, Centerville, Addison, Jonesport, Beals, Jonesboro, Roque Bluffs, Whitneyville and Machias in beautiful Washington County and I am here today to present my bill - LD 1243 An Act Regarding the Licensing of Assisted Living Facilities.
I am presenting this bill today on behalf of one of my constituents. I have known this constituent and his family for many years and when he approached me with his situation, I began thinking how I could help.
Growing up in rural Maine is really a special opportunity. You get to know your neighbors, town citizens and surrounding communities. You grow up with generations of your family surrounding you and those who move away for some time usually wish to return home. Life is simple and people are very independent and proud and asking for help is a last resort because you always feel you should be helping others.
My constituent owns an Adult Family Care Home in Harrington, Maine. With a waiting list for openings of a room in the 6-room facility, he saw the need for more quality care for aging adults and decided to invest in opening a new facility to provide opportunities for families to get assistance with their loved ones. While he was working on the construction of the facility, starting in 2021 , unbeknownst to him, a law went into effect in October of 2023 that would not allow him to open the newly built facility he was working on. He only became aware of this after all inspections were completed and he applied for his license and was denied in April of 2024.
In May 2024 I received the news that another nursing home in my area was closing. Narraguagus Bay Health Care Facility was in the heart of Milbridge and was caring for about 40 residents. This nursing facility was a big part of the community, and the residents were always out for parades and town functions and the students from the local elementary school would visit with residents for holidays and most importantly some were able to be close to their homes where family and friends could visit.
District 11 Addison, Beals, Columbia, Columbia Falls, Harrington, Jonesboro, Jonesport, Machias, Milbridge, Roque Bluffs, Whitneyville, Centerville Township, and North Washington (Part)

With this news and knowing about a brand-new facility waiting to open that would be able to keep 6 people close to home and receive great care, this bill seemed very important to put forth for consideration. The intent of this bill is not to go against the needs the Department of Health and Human Services saw when putting forth LD 475, it instead would open up an opportunity for someone who had good intentions and a proven history of great care of individuals to be able to offer their services to 6 more families in need of having someone assist them with their loved one. People do not want to think of their loved ones as a burden and in DownEast fashion individuals do not want to seem like a burden to anyone, but unfortunately, sometimes both of these things are true. The family needs assistnace as they may not be trained to provide the needed care or they themselves need to work to maintain all the other needs of everyday life. When you have to make the tough decision to move your loved one away from their home, sometimes the only home they have ever known, having an opportunity to keep them close to home and receive the good care they need is the best thing you could hope for. We all know the opportunities across the State of Maine for caring for our elderly or those who need special care are very limited. This is especially challenging in rural Maine where we are a 45% receiver of MaineCare. By allowing those who already started construction of a new facility at the same location of their current facility with the intention of licensing at the same level as their current facility the opportunity to open the fully constructed and inspection passed facility would be a wonderful gift. As a part of the licensing review there would have to be no major violations associated with the license related to the already existing and operating facility. Thank you for your time today and I would be glad to answer any questions and my constituent is here today to further describe his situation and answer any questions you may have about the facility. Sincerely,
Tiffany Strout State Representative
District 11 Addison, Beals, Columbia, Columbia Falls, Harrington, Jonesboro, Jonesport, Machias, Milbridge, Roque Bluffs, Whitneyville, Centerville Township, and North Washington (Part)
